groups.label: Early Education and State Myths
groups.summary: The origins of guardians in a luxurious state require disciplined physical and moral training, encompassing the censorship of theological poetry, constraints on musical modes and imitative drama, simple bodily regimen, and the legitimating myth of earthborn metals.
groups.rationale: All six items form a tight thematic and source sequence from the early commentary on Books II-III, addressing guardian cultivation, censorship of arts, physical training, and societal foundation myths.

groups.label: Virtues and Philosopher-Rulers
groups.summary: Civic justice and cardinal virtues establish proper governance, yet authentic philosophers are rejected like true pilots in a mutinous crew; nevertheless, those trained by mathematical abstractions toward true being must be compelled to descend and rule.
groups.rationale: These commentary entries trace the development of civic virtues and the necessity, intellectual preparation (arithmetic), and political paradoxes surrounding philosopher-kings.

groups.label: Justice, Tyranny, and Happiness
groups.summary: Socrates argues that the just soul lives well and achieves true profit and happiness, while the tyrannical ruler represents the extreme opposite, living in utter terror, enslavement, and misery.
groups.rationale: Directly links Socrates' Book I dialogue on the intrinsic happiness and profitability of justice with the commentary on the extreme misery and internal slavery of the tyrant.

groups.label: Critique of Ideal State Reforms
groups.summary: Commentary examines Plato's overarching political vision alongside its radical paradoxes—including the abolition of private property, communal family arrangements, the expulsion of poetry, and the problematic emulation of Spartan collectivism over individual genius.
groups.rationale: Groups together the late commentary essays that evaluate Plato's theoretical ideal state, including its communal paradoxes, anti-poetic epistemology, and Spartan parallels.
